description:
We want to solve a significant problem in one of several areas (data visualization, optimization, machine learning) that relates to both NASA data and how we can use AI and other creative coding to develop a solution that is both technically robust and practical.

We are interested in individuals who are passionate about solving problems using their skills in one or more of the following: environmental science, geospatial analysis, UI/UX, data science, or machine learning.
summary:
Trend Detective is a free website that lets students and the public act as data detectives with NASA climate data. They can choose a region and season to see the data for that location and time for every month since 1980, including how quickly it’s changing (corrected for autocorrelation using both a t-test and a Mann-Kendall test) with a 95% range and a simple conclusion: none, suggestive or significant.
While most free trend investigation tools only allow people to choose a location and see how a variable changes, Trend Detective also allows users to choose a variable (like air temperature being 10 °C or higher) and see how many locations on Earth experience that variable every year. Users can also apply the data to a real-world problem by using a shipping map to determine the quickest routes across the ocean every year based on NASA’s data about ocean currents, wind and sea ice - or use a tanker planner to find the most cost-effective routes based on CO₂, fuel, tolls for canals and travel time. Finally, each investigation is cross-checked using the NSIDC Sea Ice Index and NASA GISTEMP. Since actual climate investigation often involves large data downloads, creating accounts and writing code, being able to use this tool in any browser without installing anything is important.
details:
What it does and how it works

  • Data pipeline (Python): downloads NASA MERRA-2 monthly means from GES DISC (1980 to 2026-09, 561 months). It averages them onto coarser grids, weighted by area, and packs each variable into a compact Int16 binary file with a catalog.json. ECCO ocean currents and the MERRA-2 ocean fraction are processed the same way for ship routing.
  • Statistics engine (plain JavaScript, no dependencies): region averages weighted by true cell area, a least-squares slope with t-test and 95% interval, a Mann-Kendall test with autocorrelation correction and Sen’s slope, trend maps, band tracking, a “years needed to detect” estimate (Weatherhead et al. 1998), and climate velocity (Loarie et al. 2009).
    • Time series: trend line, verdict, climate stripes and the seasonal cycle.
    • Trend map: non-significant cells are hatched, so opposite trends in different places stand out.
    • Shift: fixes a value and follows the zone that has it. For example, Europe’s 10 °C zone moves north about 114 km per decade.
    • Compare regions: the same variable in two places.
    • Climate analog: where a city’s 1980s climate is found today. For Paris it is about 885 km to the northeast.
    • Sea-ice route: open-water months along Arctic shipping routes.
    • Field lineup and trend atlas: every variable at once.
    • Shipping routes: the fastest lanes each year, with a 5-year projection.
    • Tanker voyage planner: A* search on a 0.5° ocean grid using 10 m wind, ECCO currents, sea ice and canal size limits.
    • Validation view.
  • Guided procedures play step by step with narration, and any view can be exported as a figure or shared as a link.

Benefits and intended impact

  • No coding, no account, no download and no API keys, so anyone can test whether an Earth-system change is real.
  • It teaches the difference between a trend and a significant trend. A “none” result is shown as a finding, not a failure.
  • It connects climate trends to real economic decisions: shipping lanes, Arctic access, fuel use and CO₂.
  • Teachers get ready-made guided cases.

Validation

  • Global 2 m temperature trend: +0.165 °C per decade, against GISTEMP v4’s +0.208. The 95% intervals overlap, and yearly values correlate at r = 0.97.
  • September Arctic sea ice: −11.7% per decade, against NSIDC’s −12.4%, with r = 0.99.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules), Python, HTML and CSS.
  • Browser: WebGL2 for the map and 3D globe, HTML canvas for charts, and a Web Worker for routing.
  • Libraries: d3 v7.9.0, topojson-client v3.1.0, world-atlas v2.0.2 (Natural Earth coastlines).
  • Python pipeline: numpy, xarray, netCDF4, earthaccess, requests.
  • Hosting: static files on Vercel, with no backend. No special hardware.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write code and text. This is declared in the README, in source file headers and in commit trailers. The app itself calls no AI model.

What makes it creative

  • The Shift view turns the usual question around: instead of “how does this place change?”, it asks “where does this condition move?”
  • It also turns trend detection into a practical tool through year-by-year shipping routes and tanker voyage costs.
  • Results come as plain-language verdicts that use two tests, not a raw p-value.

What the team considered

  • Scientific honesty: two tests, stated limits (linear trends only, reanalysis rather than direct measurement, about 200 km grid cells), and a check against independent records.
  • Known data issue: a preliminary-data spike in precipitation over southern Italy in February 2026 is documented.
  • Accessibility: works in any browser, with plain-language definitions.
  • Performance: compact binary data and computation in the browser.
